blocks.body:
Gauss's identity $\sum_{d \mid n}\varphi(d) = n$ from [[arithmetic-functions]] packs all values of $\varphi$ into one simple sum. Can we unpack it and solve for $\varphi(n)$? More generally, if $g(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)$ for every $n$, is $f$ determined by $g$, and is there a formula?

The answer is yes. The formula uses the Möbius function $\mu$, and the right setting for it is an operation on arithmetic functions called Dirichlet convolution. Under convolution, divisor sums become products. Möbius inversion is then just division by the constant function $1$. This point of view also turns many counting problems into routine calculations.

blocks.title: Unwinding a divisor sum by hand
blocks.body:
Suppose we know $g(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)$ and want $f$. For a prime, $g(p) = f(1) + f(p)$, so $f(p) = g(p) - g(1)$. For $p^2$, $g(p^2) = f(1) + f(p) + f(p^2)$, so $f(p^2) = g(p^2) - g(p)$. For $n = pq$ with distinct primes,

$$f(pq) = g(pq) - g(p) - g(q) + g(1).$$

A pattern appears: $f(n)$ is a signed sum of values $g(n/d)$. The sign is $+$ or $-$ according to whether $d$ is a product of an even or odd number of distinct primes, and $d$ never contains a square. This is exactly what the Möbius function encodes.

blocks.title: Möbius function
blocks.body:
The Möbius function is

$$\mu(n) = \begin{cases} 1 & n = 1,\\ (-1)^k & n \text{ is a product of } k \text{ distinct primes},\\ 0 & p^2 \mid n \text{ for some prime } p. \end{cases}$$

For instance $\mu(6) = 1$, $\mu(30) = -1$, $\mu(12) = 0$. It is multiplicative, with $\mu(p) = -1$ and $\mu(p^a) = 0$ for $a \ge 2$.

blocks.title: Dirichlet convolution
blocks.body:
The Dirichlet convolution of arithmetic functions $f$ and $g$ is

$$(f*g)(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)\,g(n/d) = \sum_{ab = n} f(a)\,g(b).$$

Here $1$ denotes the constant function $1(n) = 1$, $\mathrm{id}(n) = n$, and $\varepsilon(n)$ equals $1$ if $n = 1$ and $0$ otherwise. In this notation $\tau = 1*1$, $\sigma = \mathrm{id}*1$, and Gauss's identity reads $\varphi * 1 = \mathrm{id}$.

blocks.title: The ring of arithmetic functions
blocks.body:
Convolution behaves like multiplication.

1. It is commutative, since the sum over pairs $ab = n$ is symmetric.
2. It is associative: both $(f*g)*h$ and $f*(g*h)$ evaluated at $n$ equal $\sum_{abc = n} f(a)g(b)h(c)$, the sum over ordered triples of positive integers with product $n$.
3. $\varepsilon$ is the identity: $(f*\varepsilon)(n) = f(n)$, since only $d = n$ contributes.
4. It distributes over ordinary addition of functions.

So arithmetic functions, with pointwise addition and Dirichlet convolution, form a commutative ring.

Which functions have an inverse? If $f*g = \varepsilon$, then at $n = 1$ we get $f(1)g(1) = 1$, so $f(1) \ne 0$ is necessary. It is also sufficient. Set $g(1) = 1/f(1)$, and for $n > 1$ solve $\sum_{d \mid n} f(n/d)\,g(d) = 0$ for the term with $d = n$:

$$g(n) = -\frac{1}{f(1)}\sum_{d \mid n,\ d < n} f(n/d)\,g(d).$$

This defines $g(n)$ recursively from smaller values. In particular the constant function $1$ has an inverse, and the next theorem identifies it.

Convolution also respects multiplicativity. If $f$ and $g$ are multiplicative and $\gcd(m, n) = 1$, each divisor of $mn$ is uniquely $d_1 d_2$ with $d_1 \mid m$, $d_2 \mid n$, and then $\frac{mn}{d_1 d_2} = \frac{m}{d_1}\cdot\frac{n}{d_2}$ with coprime factors. So $(f*g)(mn) = (f*g)(m)\,(f*g)(n)$. Hence $f*g$ is multiplicative, and it can be computed from prime powers via $(f*g)(p^a) = \sum_{i=0}^{a} f(p^i)\,g(p^{a-i})$.

blocks.title: Divisor sum of μ
blocks.body:
For every positive integer $n$,

$$\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d) = \begin{cases}1 & n = 1,\\ 0 & n > 1.\end{cases}$$

In other words $\mu * 1 = \varepsilon$, so $\mu$ is the Dirichlet inverse of $1$.

For $n = 1$ the sum is $\mu(1) = 1$. For $n > 1$, let $p_1, \dots, p_k$ ($k \ge 1$) be the distinct primes dividing $n$. Divisors with a repeated prime factor contribute $0$. The remaining divisors are the products of subsets of $\{p_1, \dots, p_k\}$, and a subset of size $j$ contributes $(-1)^j$. Hence

$$\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d) = \sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}(-1)^j = (1 - 1)^k = 0.$$

blocks.title: Möbius inversion formula
blocks.body:
For arithmetic functions $f$ and $g$,

$$g(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d) \ \text{ for all } n \quad\iff\quad f(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\, g(n/d) \ \text{ for all } n.$$

The left statement says $g = f * 1$ and the right says $f = g * \mu$. If $g = f*1$, then by associativity and the previous theorem

$$g*\mu = (f*1)*\mu = f*(1*\mu) = f*\varepsilon = f.$$

Conversely, if $f = g*\mu$, then $f*1 = g*(\mu*1) = g*\varepsilon = g$.

blocks.title: Using inversion
blocks.body:
Apply inversion to Gauss's identity $\varphi * 1 = \mathrm{id}$. It gives $\varphi = \mathrm{id} * \mu$, that is,

$$\varphi(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\,\frac{n}{d} = n\sum_{d \mid n}\frac{\mu(d)}{d} = n\prod_{p \mid n}\Bigl(1 - \frac1p\Bigr).$$

The last step expands the product over primes: only squarefree $d$ survive, each with sign $(-1)^{\#\text{primes}}$. This recovers the product formula for $\varphi$ without any separate inclusion–exclusion argument.

The identity $\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d) = [n = 1]$ is also a device in its own right. It turns the condition "$\gcd(a, b) = 1$" into a sum, $[\gcd(a,b) = 1] = \sum_{d \mid a,\ d \mid b}\mu(d)$. For example, the number of pairs $(a, b)$ with $1 \le a, b \le N$ and $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ is

$$\sum_{a, b \le N}\ \sum_{d \mid \gcd(a,b)}\mu(d) = \sum_{d \le N}\mu(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac Nd\Bigr\rfloor^2,$$

since for each $d$ there are $\lfloor N/d\rfloor^2$ pairs of multiples of $d$. For $N = 100$ this gives $6087$ coprime pairs out of $10000$. The proportion tends to $\sum_d \mu(d)/d^2 = 6/\pi^2 \approx 0.608$. Sieve methods start from this same identity.

Two more facts are worth knowing. If $f$ is completely multiplicative, its inverse is $\mu f$ (pointwise product), because $\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)f(d)f(n/d) = f(n)\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)$. And when functions are packaged as Dirichlet series, convolution becomes multiplication: formally $\bigl(\sum f(n)n^{-s}\bigr)\bigl(\sum g(n)n^{-s}\bigr) = \sum (f*g)(n)\,n^{-s}$. Since $1 * \mu = \varepsilon$, we get $\sum_{n \ge 1}\mu(n)n^{-s} = 1/\zeta(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, where $\zeta(s) = \sum n^{-s}$.

blocks.solution:
$60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$. Only squarefree divisors matter: $1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30$, with $\mu$ values $1, -1, -1, -1, 1, 1, 1, -1$. So

$$\varphi(60) = 60 - 30 - 20 - 12 + 10 + 6 + 4 - 2 = 16.$$

Check with the product formula: $60 \cdot \frac12 \cdot \frac23 \cdot \frac45 = 16$.

blocks.body: A binary string of length $n$ is primitive if it is not a repetition of a shorter string (for example $0101$ is not primitive, $0110$ is). How many primitive binary strings of length $6$ are there? How many necklaces of $6$ beads in two colours, considered up to rotation, are primitive?
blocks.solution:
Every binary string of length $n$ is, in exactly one way, a primitive string of some length $d \mid n$ repeated $n/d$ times. If $P(d)$ is the number of primitive strings of length $d$, then

$$\sum_{d \mid n} P(d) = 2^n.$$

By Möbius inversion, $P(n) = \sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\,2^{n/d}$. For $n = 6$, with $\mu(1) = 1$, $\mu(2) = \mu(3) = -1$, $\mu(6) = 1$:

$$P(6) = 2^6 - 2^3 - 2^2 + 2^1 = 64 - 8 - 4 + 2 = 54.$$

The $6$ rotations of a primitive string are all different (if two coincided, the string would have a shorter period). So primitive strings fall into rotation classes of size exactly $6$, and there are $54/6 = 9$ primitive necklaces. In general there are $\frac1n\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)2^{n/d}$. The same formula, with $2$ replaced by $q$, counts monic irreducible polynomials of degree $n$ over a field with $q$ elements.

blocks.body: Find a formula for $G(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k, n)$ and evaluate $G(12)$.
blocks.solution:
Group the $k$ by the value $g = \gcd(k, n)$. Writing $k = gj$, the condition $\gcd(k, n) = g$ means $1 \le j \le n/g$ and $\gcd(j, n/g) = 1$, so there are $\varphi(n/g)$ such $k$. Hence

$$G(n) = \sum_{g \mid n} g\,\varphi(n/g) = (\mathrm{id} * \varphi)(n).$$

As a convolution of multiplicative functions, $G$ is multiplicative, so it is enough to compute it on prime powers:

$$G(p^a) = \sum_{i=0}^{a} p^i\,\varphi(p^{a-i}) = p^a + \sum_{i=0}^{a-1}p^i\bigl(p^{a-i} - p^{a-i-1}\bigr) = (a+1)p^a - a\,p^{a-1}.$$

For $12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$: $G(4) = 3 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 2 = 8$ and $G(3) = 2 \cdot 3 - 1 = 5$, so $G(12) = 40$. Direct check: the gcds of $1, \dots, 12$ with $12$ are $1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 6, 1, 4, 3, 2, 1, 12$, and these add up to $40$.

blocks.body:
- Inversion needs the relation $g(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} f(d)$ for every $n$ (or at least for every divisor of the $n$ you care about), not just for one value.
- The Dirichlet inverse of $1$ is $\mu$, not the pointwise reciprocal $1/1 = 1$. Convolution inverses and pointwise inverses are different things.
- The rule "inverse of $f$ is $\mu f$" holds for completely multiplicative $f$ only. For example, the inverse of $\tau$ is $\mu * \mu$, and $(\mu*\mu)(p^2) = 1$ while $\mu(p^2)\tau(p^2) = 0$.
- Do not confuse divisor sums with summatory functions. The relation $G(x) = \sum_{n \le x} F(x/n)$ has its own inversion, $F(x) = \sum_{n \le x}\mu(n)\,G(x/n)$. It looks similar but runs over all $n \le x$, not over divisors.

The identity $\sum \mu(n)n^{-s} = 1/\zeta(s)$ is the first link between Möbius inversion and [[dirichlet-series|Dirichlet series and Euler products]]. If $P$ is the product of a finite set of primes, the number of positive integers up to $x$ with no prime factor in that set is $\sum_{d \mid P}\mu(d)\lfloor x/d\rfloor$. This is the Legendre sieve, the starting point of [[sieve-basics]]. Inverting $\log = \Lambda * 1$ gives $\Lambda = \mu * \log$, which is used throughout [[chebyshev]] and [[pnt]].

In combinatorics, Rota (1964), building on earlier work of Weisner and Philip Hall, developed a general theory of Möbius functions and Möbius inversion on any locally finite partially ordered set. The divisors of $n$, ordered by divisibility, form one such poset. The subsets of a finite set, ordered by inclusion, form another, and there Möbius inversion is exactly inclusion–exclusion (see [[counting]]). When $n$ is squarefree the two pictures coincide: a divisor $d$ of $n$ corresponds to the set $S$ of primes dividing it, and $\mu(d) = (-1)^{|S|}$ is exactly the inclusion–exclusion sign.

1. Show that $\sum_{d \mid n}|\mu(d)| = 2^{\omega(n)}$, where $\omega(n)$ is the number of distinct primes dividing $n$.
2. Show that $\sum_{d \mid n}\mu(d)\,\tau(n/d) = 1$ for every $n$.
3. Prove that $\sum_{d^2 \mid n}\mu(d)$ equals $1$ if $n$ is squarefree and $0$ otherwise.
4. Find the Dirichlet inverse of $\sigma$ and describe its values on prime powers.
